hero.title: The Race to Save Space
hero.content: Ensuring peace and sustainability in the final frontier

sputnik.title: Ready. Set. Blast off.
sputnik.content:
The Space Age dawned on 4 October 1957, when Sputnik 1, the world’s first satellite successfully launched and orbited Earth.

Lasting three weeks, this beeping metal sphere, the size of a beach ball, kicked off a technological race that would forever change humanity’s relationship with space.

items.title: Sputnik 1 becomes first satellite to orbit Earth, revolutionizing global communications.
The UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space is established.
Yuri Gagarin makes history as first human in space.
Valentina Tereshkova makes history as first woman in space.
Outer Space Treaty establishes first multilateral legal framework on the peaceful exploration of space.
Apollo 11 achieves first manned moon landing, marking humanity's first venture to another celestial body.
The Apollo-Soyuz joint mission achieves first international space docking, uniting Soviet and American crews at height of Cold War.
Dennis Tito makes headlines as first space tourist, shelling out USD 20 million for the out-of-galaxy experience; he plans to go again with his wife.
Ax-1 launches first all-private crewed mission to International Space Station, a step forward in commercial space exploration.

intro.title: Balancing Innovation, Sustainability and Risk
intro.content: The future of space depends on countries working together to balance national interests, commercial opportunities, and the common good of humanity.

keySpaceTreaties.today: Today, five UN space treaties remain the cornerstone of space law.

intro.title:
Your Daily Life is
Powered by Space
intro.content: Today, near space is an extension of Earth’s environment, a technological bridgehead inextricably tied to our daily lives.

slides.title: Satellites power air, land and sea navigation, weather forecasting, tv broadcasts, internet access, global commerce, and much more.

intro.title: Space technology also benefits communities worldwide
intro.content: Satellites play a vital role in the Sustainable Development Goals, humanity’s shared blueprint for a better future for people and the planet. Here are just some ways how:

cards.title: Zero Hunger
cards.content: Global Navigation Satellite Systems and Earth Observation enable precision agriculture for optimized crop yields.

cards.title: Good Health and Well-being
cards.content: Space-derived data is used to monitor and map yellow fever mosquito populations.

cards.title: Reduced Inequalities
cards.content: Space technologies connect remote and isolated communities to services, education, and work opportunities.

cards.title: Climate Action
cards.content: Satellites monitor climate patterns, forecast weather, and aid in disaster management and response.

intro.title: One Small Step, One Giant Leap
intro.content: In recent years, a surge in space activities has ushered in a new era of innovation.

satelliteLaunches.intro: Driven by advancing technology, lower launch costs and smaller satellites, private companies have entered the scene, dramatically changing space utilization — and our night sky.
satelliteLaunches.title: In a Nutshell: Satellite Launches

right.bottom: satellites launched, marking the beginning of an exponential growth trend
satellites could fill our skies as launch costs drop, private investment surges, and technology advances.

years.content: Well over a million satellites could fill our night sky in just a matter of years as launch technology gets cheaper along with technological breakthroughs and private sector involvement Annual launches could hit millions, boosting connectivity but straining space sustainability

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.content: Most satellite constellations are just 500 km above our heads. That’s approximately the distance from [city1] to [city2].

weHaveAProblem.title:
Humankind,
we have a problem
weHaveAProblem.content: The fast-growing number of objects — satellites, defunct spacecraft, and debris — is a growing hazard for space operations.

intro.content: Left unregulated, increasing space traffic and junk could turn the very technology we rely on against itself and stop humanity in its tracks.

stats.title: Space debris objects in Earth’s lower orbit

debrisDidYouKnow.title: Did you know?
debrisDidYouKnow.subtitle:
10000 tonnes
of space trouble
debrisDidYouKnow.content: The combined weight of human-made objects in space debris is the weight of the Eiffel Tower – a staggering 10,000 tonnes orbiting our planet!

slides.title:
The Emerging Race
for Space Resources
slides.content: From valuable metals like platinum, nickel, and cobalt within asteroids to frozen water on celestial bodies, space resources present significant economic potential.
Today, commercial activities are claiming an ever-growing share of the space economy.

statsSection.title:
Global
space market
statsSection.content:
This shift raises
critical questions.

Without international principles on space resources, economic incentives pose risks for potential conflict, environmental degradation, and widening inequalities. Whoever dominates this frontier may shape humanity's cosmic future.

intro.title: Shaping a Common Path Forward
intro.content: The cosmos is vast, and its benefits are immense. But Earth's orbits are limited.

slides.subtitle: As space activities intensify amid geopolitical tensions, implementing and expanding space laws is urgent. Humanity has a moral imperative to exercise stewardship together towards the sustainable, peaceful use of space.

orbitalCleanup.title: The Great Orbital Clean-up
orbitalCleanup.content: Space debris removal — and space traffic coordination — requires a whole new approach, combining preventive measures with active cleanup efforts.

cards.title: Debris mitigation
cards.content: Designing satellites to minimize the creation of new debris.

cards.title: Active debris removal
cards.content: Developing sustainable solutions and technologies to remove existing debris.

slides.content: Even small debris objects can cause significant, if not catastrophic, damage

slides.title: Too close for comfort
slides.content: Debris can travel at 7.5 km/s (27,000 km/h), 20 times faster than a gun shot.

slides.title: No small matter
slides.content: A single nut or bolt hitting a spacecraft can release a similar quantity of energy to a hand grenade, shattering a satellite or spacecraft into pieces.

cascadeEffect.title: Space junk is a self-perpetuating problem
cascadeEffect.content: Collisions between objects create more debris, increasing the likelihood of future collisions. This cascade effect, known as the Kessler Syndrome, could make certain orbital regions unusable.
cascadeEffect.interaction: A single collision can generate thousands of pieces of space debris, leading to even more debris. Move your mouse into the circle to visualize the domino effect.
cascadeEffect.interactionMobile: A single collision can generate thousands of pieces of space debris, leading to even more debris. Tap into the circle to visualize the domino effect.

slides.title: SOS
slides.content: There’s more peril to this galactic picture…and saving our outer space

slides.title: The Growing Threat to Nations
slides.content: Military confrontation in space is no longer science fiction.
The increasing reliance on space-based services for security, defense, and daily operations combined with new space actors, poses new threats to peace.
A large-scale attack on satellites, for instance, could:

cards.title: Disrupt air, land, and marine navigation
cards.content: Modern transportation systems worldwide depend on satellites to navigate safely.

cards.title: Disrupt internet access
cards.content: Satellites ensure global communications and internet connectivity.

cards.title: Destabilize financial markets
cards.content: Global financial systems need satellite timing for transactions to work.

slides.content: Preventing warfare in space through strengthened international frameworks is one of the bold commitments within the UN’s Pact for the Future, adopted by world leaders in 2024.

intro.content: Ensuring the equitable, peaceful and sustainable use of space requires further international agreements to match today’s complex realities. International consensus continues to grow, with guiding frameworks already adopted on issues like space debris and the long-term sustainability of outer space through the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space.

pactForFuture.content: An important step in this direction, world leaders adopted the Pact for the Future in 2024, committing to the safe and sustainable exploration of outer space — a promise that must now be realized.

expansion.title: In the 0 minutes that you’ve been on this page, the radius of the universe has expanded by approximately 0 million kilometers—and its volume by much more.
expansion.content:
A reminder of the vast cosmic scale and
how small our own crowded orbital space truly is.

share.copy: Every minute, the universe expands by over 42,000 kilometers—an immense reminder of the vastness of space. Yet, our own orbital space is becoming dangerously crowded. Act now to protect the final frontier. #OurCommonFuture

slides.content: The Next Giant Leap is Ours to Shape
We must act now and together to secure our cosmic future for all humanity.

popup.title: Fraud Alert
popup.content:
Beware of scams implying association with the United Nations.

The United Nations has been made aware of various correspondences, being circulated via e-mail, from Internet web sites, text messages and via regular mail or facsimile, falsely stating that they are issued by, or in association with the United Nations and/or its officials. These scams, which may seek to obtain money and/or in many cases personal details from the recipients of such correspondence, are fraudulent.

The United Nations wishes to warn the public at large about these fraudulent activities being perpetrated purportedly in the name of the Organisation, and/or its officials, through different fraud schemes.

  • The United Nations does not charge a fee at any stage of its recruitment process (application, interview, processing, training) or other fee, or request information on applicants’ bank accounts. To apply for a job go to careers.un.org and click on Vacancies. See more on employment-related fraud.
  • The United Nations does not charge a fee at any stage of its procurement process (supplier registration, bids submission) or other fee. Visit the Procurement Division to see the latest business opportunities with the United Nations.
  • The United Nations does not request any information related to bank accounts or other private information.
  • The United Nations does not offer prizes, awards, funds, certificates, automated teller machine (ATM) cards, compensation for Internet fraud, or scholarships, or conduct lotteries.
  • The United Nations does not approve military vacations or pensions, or release packages in exchange for a fee.

The United Nations strongly recommends that the recipients of solicitations, such as those described above exercise extreme caution in respect of such solicitations. Financial loss and identity theft could result from the transfer of money or personal information to those issuing such fraudulent correspondence. Victims of such scams may also report them to their local law enforcement authorities for appropriate action.

Not an official document. For information only.

popup.title: Privacy Notice
popup.content:
UN.ORG Data Protection and Privacy Notice
This notice applies to all websites within the UN.ORG domain name (“UN websites”).
Your privacy and the protection of personal data are important to the United Nations (UN). This data protection and privacy notice describes the UN’s policy concerning the gathering and sharing of personal data through UN websites. By visiting a UN website, you are accepting the practices described in this policy.

Secretary-General’s Bulletin
UN websites are guided by a set of principles on personal data protection and privacy that were established by the Secretary‑General’s Bulletin enshrining the Data protection and privacy policy for the Secretariat of the United Nations (ST/SGB/2024/1).

What information does the United Nations collect?

Normal website usage
In general, you can browse a UN website without telling us who you are or revealing any personal information about yourself.
Our systems automatically gather some anonymous information about visitors during general browsing. This includes technical network information such as the IP (Internet Protocol) address you appear to be connecting from, its domain name, the type of browser you are employing, the operating system, and other information such as the website from which you reached a UN website, the files you downloaded from UN websites, the pages you visited on UN websites, and the dates/times of those visits to UN websites.

UN websites may, from time to time, avail of web analytics services provided by third parties for the purposes of evaluating the use of UN websites, compiling reports on website activity for website operators and for intergovernmental organs requesting such statistical reports, as well as for other services relating to website activity and internet usage. The information collected by such third parties, including your IP address, may be stored on the servers of such third parties and be subject to their respective privacy policies as well as any laws and regulations applicable to them.

Personal data
UN websites only collect personal data with your knowledge.
If you register for a newsletter, login to certain UN websites, order a book or other merchandise, request information, provide feedback, apply for a job, join a discussion group, or join an electronic mailing list, you may be asked to provide personal information such as your name, postal address and/or e-mail address.

Joining electronic discussion groups may mean that other participants of the discussion group (including non-UN employees) will see personal information that you have volunteered to provide. For open discussion groups, this information will be public.

If you conduct a transaction such as ordering merchandise or booking a tour of United Nations Headquarters, you may also be asked to provide your credit card details. These details are transferred to a secure, online payment service, hosted by a third party. Credit card information is not retained by the UN.

Cookies
UN websites may use cookies to provide statistics that help us to give you the best experience of our sites.

What does the United Nations do with the information it collects?

Normal web site usage
Information is gathered by automated means during general browsing of a UN website through the use of “cookies” or “web beacons”. Information such as the IP address associated with your connection to the internet and the pages accessed is used to analyze trends and usage of that UN website and to improve the usefulness of the site. Your IP address is not connected with any personal data.

Personal data
The UN may use the personal data you provide for the purposes for which it is collected, such as:

  • Contacting you – either in response to a query or suggestion, or to mail newsletters, documents, publications, etc. to you.
  • Managing and processing your job application.
  • Confirming your purchases and registrations on the site.
  • Obtaining payment for purchases through the site (via credit card).
  • 'Remembering' your online profile and preferences.
  • Helping you quickly find information that is relevant to you based on your interests and helping us create site content most relevant to you.
  • Undertaking statistical analysis.

What if I don’t want to provide personal data?
Providing personal data on a UN website is optional. If you choose not to provide personal data, you may not be able to carry out certain actions such as purchase items, register for a newsletter, or apply for a job.

How does the United Nations protect your personal data?
We never sell any information collected through UN websites. We do not regularly share any personal data collected on the UN website to any third party, with the exception of information transferred securely to a third-party service provider, such as a credit card processor in connection with a purchase made through a UN website. We employ a range of technologies and security measures to protect the information maintained on our systems from loss, misuse, unauthorized access or disclosure, alteration, or destruction.

All United Nations staff who have access to, and are associated with the processing of personal data, are obliged to comply with the rules concerning the classification and handling of all United Nations data, including with respect to the confidentiality of personal data they handle in their official capacity. These include the rules enshrined in ST/SGB/2024/1.

How long does the United Nations retain your personal data?
Your personal data will be kept only as long as it is necessary for the purposes set out in this notice. How long personal information is stored for depends on the personal information in question and what it is being used for, as well as whether there is any administrative or regulatory requirement for retaining the personal information.

How do you make requests concerning your personal data?
In some cases, you can request modification or deletion of your personal data directly by returning to the web page where you first provided the information and following the instructions provided. When such option is not available, you can submit the following requests concerning personal data collected by UN websites for consideration by sending an email to us via the Contact page.

  • Request whether any personal data relating to you is being processed.
  • Request access to the personal data relating to you that is being processed.
  • Request to rectify, complete, delete, or stop processing personal data relating to you.

You can find more information about the procedure concerning such requests in ST/SGB/2024/1.

Notification of changes
The present notice is subject to amendment at the discretion of the United Nations. Any changes will be posted on this page.

Privileges and immunities
Nothing in or relating to the present notice shall be deemed a waiver, express or implied, of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations, including its subsidiary organs.

Contact
For questions or queries regarding this data protection and privacy policy, please contact us via the Contact page.
